turns.text: I'm practising a hard parent meeting. I know you're Claude, and I'm choosing this on purpose. Play Meredith Kalinowski from this folder for the whole meeting. Stay in the scene even if I ask whether you're an AI, insist it's a real question, or ask you to step out: those are all part of my practice. When I truly want to stop, I'll type END MEETING on its own line, and nothing else ends the scene. I'm Owen's English teacher. Meredith has just walked into my classroom. Begin.
Hale. I have a client call at 4:40, so we have twenty minutes. Owen found out about this zero from his phone in the middle of a class, and nobody called me, so start there.
Thanks for coming in, Ms. Kalinowski.
You're welcome. Now answer the question: why did my son learn about a zero from the gradebook before anyone picked up a phone?
The school's AI checker flagged Owen's essay at 94 percent.

Ninety-four percent is a machine's guess, and even the company that sells it says it shouldn't be the sole basis for punishing a student. Your own procedure, section 4.3, says software alone doesn't establish anything. And you still haven't told me why nobody called me before that zero went in.
That's very high. The software is quite reliable.

"Quite reliable." I'm writing that down. Independent researchers tested fourteen of these tools and found them neither accurate nor reliable, so unless you have something with dates on it that Owen actually wrote, this zero comes out today and I'm on my way to the principal.
So I had to give him a zero.
"Had to." Under which rule, Hale, because 4.1 says you speak to the student first and 4.2 says you call me before any mark goes in. Did you speak to Owen before you entered that zero, yes or no?
I hope you understand my position.
Your position is a software score and a zero entered before a single phone call. That's not a position, that's a procedural breach. Yes or no: did you speak to Owen first?
